Mukta Sharma, Soledad Urrutia, Alexandru Voloc, Hubert Wang, Rajendra Yadav, Kouadio Yeboue, and Askar Yedilbayev are professionals associated with various regional and country offices of the World Health Organization (WHO), representing regions such as Europe, South-East Asia, the Americas, Africa, and specific countries like Moldova and Madagascar. 2. Funding for the initiatives discussed is acknowledged from the Bristol Myers Squibb Foundation, the Republic of Korea, and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). 3. Comorbidity refers to the simultaneous presence of another disease or health condition in a person diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB). 4. Disorders due to substance use, as defined by the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), encompass conditions arising from the use of psychoactive substances, including certain medications. These disorders are categorized into alcohol use disorders and drug use disorders, excluding nicotine. 5. A health-related risk factor is any condition, disease, or behavior that increases the likelihood of developing TB. 6. High-quality healthcare is defined as safe, effective, and patient-centered services that are timely, equitable, integrated, and efficient. 7. Multimorbidity refers to the presence of two or more concurrent diseases or health conditions in a person with TB. 8. Operational research focuses on improving program performance, assessing the feasibility, effectiveness, or impact of new interventions, and guiding policy recommendations. 9. People-centered services adopt a human rights-based approach to care, emphasizing the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities as active participants in trusted health systems. These services are organized around the comprehensive needs of people rather than individual diseases. 10. Primary care is a fundamental process in the health system that ensures accessible, continuous, comprehensive, and coordinated patient-focused care at the first point of contact. 11. Primary health care is a whole-of-society approach aimed at maximizing health and well-being through three components: primary care and essential public health functions, multisectoral policy and action, and empowered people and communities. 12. Social determinants of health are non-medical factors influencing health outcomes, such as income, education, food security, housing, social inclusion, and access to quality healthcare. 13. Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this document, TB disease is used to distinguish it from TB infection. 14. TB infection is a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of active TB disease. 15. Universal health coverage ensures access to high-quality essential health services, including preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care, without financial hardship. 16. Globally, TB remains one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent. Addressing TB comorbidities and health-related risk factors, such as HIV, alcohol use disorders, undernutrition, smoking, diabetes, mental disorders, silicosis, and viral hepatitis, is critical to ending the TB epidemic. 17. Integrated, patient-centered care and prevention for TB, including HIV-associated TB and other comorbidities, are key components of the WHO End TB Strategy. 18. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated TB-related challenges by increasing poverty, undernutrition, mental health burdens, and stigma, while also disrupting healthcare services. This highlights the need for integrated, evidence-based care models. 19. Collaborative action on TB and comorbidities can improve resource efficiency, reduce healthcare visits, address health system fragmentation, and enhance health outcomes. 20. The WHO Framework for collaborative action on TB and comorbidities supports evidence-informed, people-centered services to address TB and multimorbidity comprehensively. 21. Key health-related risk factors driving the TB epidemic globally include diabetes, alcohol use disorders, HIV, smoking, and undernutrition. These factors vary in impact across countries. 22. Alcohol use disorders triple the risk of TB disease and accounted for 740,000 new TB cases in 2020. People with TB who consume alcohol are twice as likely to experience poor treatment outcomes. 23. Diabetes increases the risk of TB disease by two to three times and is associated with a higher risk of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Coordinated care is essential for managing both conditions effectively. 24. People living with HIV are at an 18-fold higher risk of developing TB compared to the general population. TB remains a leading cause of hospitalization and death among individuals with HIV. 25. Collaborative TB/HIV activities, including integrated service delivery and burden reduction, have saved an estimated 9 million lives between 2005 and 2020.
